cards.key: Heat grows with the square of the current. That is why electricity is transmitted at high voltage and low current.

cards.p: A source delivers a power of P = ε·I to the circuit. Of this, I²·r turns into heat in the internal resistance, and I²·R reaches the external resistor: ε·I = I²·R + I²·r.
cards.key: Going further: the power delivered to the external resistor is greatest when R = r. In a short circuit (R ≈ 0) it is zero.

once.soru: Why does a battery that runs for a long time heat up?

secenekler.neden: The current also passes through the battery's internal resistance. The power used there is P = I²·r. So in a time t, an energy of I²·r·t turns into heat inside the battery.
The heat forms inside the battery itself.
A battery's voltage does not increase as it is used.

cards.p: On the bill, energy is measured in kilowatt-hours. A device that runs for 1 hour at a power of 1 kW uses 1 kWh of energy. The amount to pay is the kWh multiplied by the unit price.

cards.key: 1 kWh is 3.6 million J. If a 2 kW heater runs 3 hours a day for 30 days, it uses 180 kWh. If the unit price is 3 TL, the cost is 540 TL.

etk.soru: Change the device's power, the daily use, and the unit price. What is your 30-day bill?

cards.p: 220 V, 1100 W on a label says that 1100 W is used at 220 V. This gives I = P/V = 5 A and R = V²/P = 44 Ω.

once.soru: You connect two identical bulbs in parallel. How does each glow compared with a single bulb?

secenekler.neden: Each bulb still gets the battery's full voltage, and its power stays P. The battery, however, delivers twice the current.
Dimming happens in a series connection.
Since the voltage does not increase, the power does not increase either.

once.soru: You turn off the lamp in the living room. The fridge keeps running. Why?

secenekler.neden: Each device has its own branch. When one is switched on or off, the other is not affected.
In series, turning off the lamp would break the circuit, and the fridge would stop too.
All the devices in a home get the same 220 V.

cards.p: A fuse is connected in series with the live wire and cuts the circuit when the current limit (e.g. 16 A) is exceeded. An overload or a short circuit can heat the cables and start a fire.

cards.key: Do not touch an outlet with wet hands. Do not use damaged cables, and do not overload a power strip.

once.soru: Current leaked onto the metal casing of a washing machine. If the casing is grounded, where does the current go?

secenekler.neden: Grounding is a path with very small resistance. The leakage current flows through it instead of through you.
On a grounded casing, the current chooses the ground wire, which has very small resistance.
Leaked current always finds a path. Grounding makes that path safe.

cards.p: The ratio of useful energy to energy used is called efficiency. An incandescent bulb converts about 5% of the energy into light. An LED gives the same light with much less power.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='88' y='52' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='bold'>Filament 60 W</text><rect x='95' y='36' width='10.5' height='24' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.8' stroke='none' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='105.5' y='36' width='199.5' height='24' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='none' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='215' y='52' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>≈ 95% heat</text><text x='88' y='102' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='bold'>LED ≈ 9 W</text><rect x='95' y='86' width='10.5' height='24' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.8' stroke='none' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='105.5' y='86' width='21.0' height='24' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='none' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='134.5' y='102' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>same light, much less heat</text><rect x='95' y='126' width='12' height='12' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.8' stroke='none' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='112' y='136' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)'>light (useful)</text><rect x='200' y='126' width='12' height='12' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='none' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='217' y='136' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)'>heat (loss)</text><text x='160' y='165' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Efficiency = useful energy / energy used</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>incandescent ≈ 5%, LED much higher</text></svg>
cards.key: Efficiency can never exceed 100%. A roughly 9 W LED is enough in place of a 60 W incandescent bulb.

cards.p:
• W = V·I·t and P = V·I = I²R = V²/R.
• I²R is used in series, V²/R in parallel.
• Power sets the brightness.
• 1 kWh is 3.6×106 J.
• Home wiring is parallel.
• A fuse protects the cable. An RCD and grounding protect people.

quiz.q: In how many seconds does a 2000 W kettle heat 1.5 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C? (Specific heat of water 4200 J/kg·°C, no heat loss)
quiz.e: The heat needed is Q = m·c·ΔT = 1.5·4200·80 = 504 000 J. The electrical energy equals P·t. So t = 504 000 / 2000 = 252 s (about 4.2 minutes).

quiz.q: Does each expression or unit give energy or power? Put it in the right group.
quiz.e: Power is energy per unit time. Its unit is the watt, that is J/s, and it is found with P = V·I = I²·R. Multiplying power by time gives energy: W = V·I·t and Q = I²·R·t. The kWh is also a unit of energy, because it is power multiplied by time.

quiz.q: Match each home electrical safety measure with its job.
ciftler: Cuts the circuit on excess current
Carries leakage current from casing to ground
Each device gets the same 220 V
quiz.e: A fuse opens the circuit when the current limit is exceeded. A residual-current device compares the current going out on the live wire with the current returning on the neutral. Grounding takes leakage current to the ground instead of through you. In parallel wiring, each device gets the same voltage.

quiz.q: Identical bulbs K and L are connected in parallel with each other. This pair is connected in series with an identical bulb M and attached to an ideal battery. What is the order of brightness?
quiz.e: The total current I passes through M, and I/2 passes through each of K and L. Since P = I²R, the power of M is 4 times that of K or L.
y: K and L on the parallel branches share the current. So less current passes through each of them than through M on the main branch.
M on the main branch carries the total current, and each parallel branch gets half of it. So M glows brighter.
Since K and L are identical and in parallel, they draw equal currents and glow equally.

manyetizma.title: Magnetism
manyetizma.summary: Magnets, the magnetic field of a current, and forces in a field.

cards.p: A magnet attracts materials such as iron. A magnet has two poles, N and S. The N end of a hanging magnet turns north. Like poles repel each other, and opposite poles attract.

cards.h: A single pole cannot be isolated
cards.p: Every piece of a broken magnet still has two poles. Magnetism comes from the tiny magnets in atoms lining up in the same direction. That is why an N or S pole is never found on its own.

cards.p: The region where a magnet has an effect is called a magnetic field. The field is shown with B, and its unit is the tesla. Field lines are closed curves and run from N to S outside the magnet. Where the lines are dense, the field is strong.

cards.h: Earth's magnetic field and the compass
cards.p: Earth is like a giant magnet. Since the N end of a compass points north, there is a magnetic S pole near geographic north. These poles do not coincide exactly, and the angle between them is called the declination.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='110' y1='34' x2='110' y2='176' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><circle cx='110' cy='105' r='58' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M122,160 C202,190 202,20 122,50' fill='none' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><polygon points='182.0,100.0 186.0,108.0 178.0,108.0' fill='var(--c5)'/><path d='M98,160 C18,190 18,20 98,50' fill='none' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><polygon points='38.0,100.0 42.0,108.0 34.0,108.0' fill='var(--c5)'/><g transform='rotate(10 110 105)'><rect x='101' y='72' width='18' height='33' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='101' y='105' width='18' height='33' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='110' y='93' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>S</text><text x='110' y='126' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>N</text></g><text x='110' y='22' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>geographic N (magnetic S)</text><text x='110' y='194' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>geographic S (magnetic N)</text><circle cx='252' cy='95' r='30' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><polygon points='252,69 258,95 246,95' fill='var(--c2)'/><polygon points='252,121 258,95 246,95' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='252' y='52' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>compass</text><text x='252' y='148' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>N end points to</text><text x='252' y='163' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>geographic north</text></svg>
cards.key: The magnetic poles slowly move. That is why the declination changes over the years.

once.soru: The N end of a compass points north. Which magnetic pole is at Earth's geographic north?

secenekler.neden: The N end of the needle is attracted by the opposite pole. So there is a magnetic S pole at geographic north.
Like poles repel each other. If there were an N pole there, the N end of the needle would turn south.
Earth behaves like a giant magnet and has two poles.

cards.p: Earth's magnetic field is also tilted toward the ground. The angle that a needle turning in a vertical plane makes with the horizontal is called the inclination. This angle is 0° at the magnetic equator and 90° at the poles.
cards.key: Declination is measured in the horizontal plane, and inclination in the vertical plane. The inclination is 0° near the equator and 90° at the magnetic poles.

once.soru: At the north magnetic pole, how does the N end of a compass needle that can turn in a vertical plane sit?

secenekler.neden: At the north magnetic pole the field lines enter the ground vertically, and the inclination is 90°. At the south magnetic pole, the N end of the needle points straight up.
The needle sits horizontal at the magnetic equator.
That happens somewhere between the equator and the pole.

cards.p: Materials that are strongly attracted to a magnet and can be magnetized are called ferromagnetic. Iron, nickel, and cobalt are among them. Aluminum is attracted very weakly, and copper is repelled very weakly.

cards.key: Aluminum is a paramagnetic material. Copper, bismuth, and water are diamagnetic. Permanent magnets are made only from ferromagnetic materials.

etk.soru: A ferromagnetic material is strongly attracted, a paramagnetic one weakly attracted, and a diamagnetic one weakly repelled. Which is this material?
ogeler: Copper is diamagnetic. It does not stick to a magnet.
Bismuth is one of the strongest diamagnetic materials.

once.soru: You bring a magnet close to a copper wire. What happens?

secenekler.neden: Copper is repelled very weakly, and this effect cannot be seen by eye.
The strongly attracted ones are iron, nickel, and cobalt.
The repulsion of copper is very weak.

cards.h: Field of a straight current-carrying wire
cards.p: A wire carrying current creates a circular field around itself. In the right-hand rule, the thumb shows the direction of the current and the curled fingers show the direction of the field. The field is found with B = 2k·I/d.

once.soru: You double the number of turns of a coil. The current and length are the same. What happens to the field inside?

secenekler.neden: Every turn contributes to the field. So the field is directly proportional to the number of turns.
The field gets stronger as the turns increase.
The field depends on the number of turns.

cards.p: When a soft iron core is placed inside the solenoid, the field becomes many times stronger. This is called an electromagnet. When the current is cut, the magnetism disappears. The strength of an electromagnet increases with the number of turns and the current.

cards.h: Force on a wire in a field
cards.p: A force acts on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field: F = B·I·L·sinθ. If the wire is parallel to the field the force is zero, and if it is perpendicular the force is greatest. In the right-hand rule, the four fingers show B, the thumb shows I, and the palm shows F.

cards.p: If two parallel wires carry currents in the same direction, the wires attract each other. If they carry currents in opposite directions, they repel each other. The two forces are equal: F/L = 2k·I₁·I₂/d.

once.soru: Two wires side by side carry currents in the same direction. What do the wires do?

secenekler.neden: Each wire feels a force in the field of the other. Currents in the same direction attract each other.
Currents in opposite directions repel.
Every wire carrying current creates a field. The other wire feels a force in this field.

cards.p: A magnetic field exerts a force only on a moving charge: F = q·v·B·sinθ. No force acts on a charge that is at rest or moving parallel to the field. An electron is pushed in the opposite direction.

once.soru: You place an electron at rest next to a magnet. Does a magnetic force act on it?

secenekler.neden: The magnetic force acts only on a moving charge. If v = 0, then F = 0.
A magnetic field does not attract a charge at rest.
A magnetic field does not repel a charge at rest.

cards.h: A charge entering perpendicular to the field moves in a circle
cards.p: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity and changes only the direction of the velocity. So the charge moves in a circle: r = m·v/(q·B). This force does no work, and the kinetic energy does not change.

once.soru: What happens over time to the speed of a charge that enters perpendicular to the field?

secenekler.neden: The force is perpendicular to the velocity. It changes only the direction and does not make the speed larger or smaller.
A force perpendicular to the velocity does no work. So the kinetic energy does not increase.
A force perpendicular to the velocity does not slow the charge down.

cards.p: Opposite forces act on the opposite sides of a current-carrying loop between magnets, and the loop turns. The commutator reverses the current every half turn. A motor converts electricity into motion.

etk.soru: Explore the parts of an electric motor.

noktalar.acik: This is the north pole of the magnet. The field lines leave from here.
This is the south pole of the magnet. The field lines enter here.
The field between the poles points from N to S.
Here you see the cross-section of the loop. The current flows in (×) on the left side and out (•) on the right side. Since the currents are opposite, the forces are opposite too.
A force of F = B·I·L acts on each side. The opposite forces on the two sides form a force couple.
The force couple turns the loop. The commutator reverses the current every half turn, and the rotation continues in the same direction.

cards.p:
• Like poles repel, opposite poles attract. There is no single pole.
• A current creates a field: B = 2k·I/d, B = 4πk·N·I/L.
• For parallel wires, F/L = 2k·I₁·I₂/d.
• The force is F = B·I·L·sinθ and F = q·v·B·sinθ.
• A charge entering perpendicular moves in a circle.

quiz.q: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. What is the magnetic field 5 cm from the wire in μT? (k = 10<sup>−7</sup> T·m/A)
quiz.e: B = 2k·I/d = 2·10<sup>−7</sup>·10/0.05 = 4·10<sup>−5</sup> T = 40 μT. If you forget to convert d to meters, you get a result 100 times too small.

quiz.q: A wire carrying current to the right in the plane of the page sits in a uniform magnetic field pointing into the page (⊗). In which direction is the force on the wire?
o: Up, in the plane of the page
Down, in the plane of the page
quiz.e: In the right-hand rule, the four fingers are held in the direction of B (into the page) and the thumb in the direction of I (to the right). In this case the palm faces up. The force is perpendicular to both I and B.
y: You found the opposite direction. Point your four fingers along B and your thumb along I. The palm shows the direction of the force.
The force must be perpendicular to the field. It cannot be in the same direction as the field.
The wire is perpendicular to the field (sinθ = 1). So the force is not zero. It is at its greatest.

quiz.q: Match each situation with its result.
ciftler: Parallel wires, currents in the same direction
Parallel wires, currents in opposite directions
Charge moving parallel to the field
Charge entering perpendicular to the field
quiz.e: Parallel wires carrying currents in the same direction attract each other, and those carrying currents in opposite directions repel. A force of F = q·v·B·sinθ acts on a moving charge. For a charge moving parallel to the field, sinθ = 0. For a charge entering perpendicular to the field, the force is perpendicular to the velocity, so the charge moves in a circle.

quiz.q: An electron entering perpendicular to the field moves in a circle of radius r. If the magnetic field is doubled while its speed stays the same, what happens to the radius and the period?
quiz.e: r = m·v/(q·B) and T = 2πm/(q·B). Both are inversely proportional to B. So when B doubles, both are halved.
y: The period T = 2πm/(q·B) also depends on B. When B increases, the period gets shorter.
Since r = m·v/(q·B), when B grows the radius does not grow. It shrinks.
Since the force q·v·B grows, the path bends more. So the radius changes.

induksiyon-ac.title: Electromagnetic induction and alternating current
induksiyon-ac.summary: Learn about flux, Faraday's and Lenz's laws, the generator, AC, the transformer, and transmission.

cards.p: The measure of the field lines passing through a surface is called magnetic flux (Φ). Flux is found with Φ = B·A·cosθ. θ is the angle between B and the normal to the surface. The unit of flux is the weber.

once.soru: You hold a loop parallel to the field lines. What is the flux through the loop?

secenekler.neden: The lines do not pass through the loop. They flow past it. In this case θ = 90° and cos90° = 0.
The flux is greatest when the loop is perpendicular to the field.
In the parallel position, no line passes through the loop.

cards.p: If the flux changes, an emf forms in the coil. According to Faraday's law, ε = −N·ΔΦ/Δt. If the flux is large but constant, the emf is zero.

once.soru: Without touching the magnet, you rotate the coil in place. Does an emf form?

secenekler.neden: When the loop rotates, θ and the flux change, so an emf forms. A generator works this way too.
Not only B but also the angle changes the flux.
Rotating the coil also changes the flux.

cards.p: The induced current opposes the change in flux that creates it. If you bring an N pole closer, that face of the loop becomes N and repels the magnet. If you pull it away, that face becomes S and attracts the magnet.

cards.p: If the flux is increasing, the induced current produces a field in the opposite direction. If it is decreasing, it produces a field in the same direction. With the right thumb along this field, the curled fingers show the direction of the current.

once.soru: The field through a loop is decreasing. In which direction is the field of the induced current?

secenekler.neden: The current opposes the decrease and supports the weakening field.
An opposite field forms when the field is increasing.
Since the flux changes, a current and its field form.

cards.p: An emf forms between the ends of a rod of length L moving in a magnetic field: ε = B·L·v. If a rod sliding on rails completes the circuit, a current flows in the circuit.

cards.p: When the current in a coil changes, its own flux changes too, and the coil produces an emf against this: ε = −L·ΔI/Δt. L is the self-inductance, and its unit is the henry.
cards.key: A coil resists the change in the current, not its value. At constant current only the resistance of the wire remains. The L here is not a length.

once.soru: You close the switch in a circuit with a coil. How does the current rise?

secenekler.neden: The coil produces an emf against the rise of the current. So the current takes some time to rise.
A coil resists a change in current and does not allow a sudden rise.
A coil slows the change, but the current eventually reaches its steady value.

cards.p: A generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. As the coil rotates in the field, the flux increases and decreases. The emf also reverses direction like a sine curve. This is called alternating current (AC).
cards.key: The peak emf is εmax = N·B·A·ω (ω = 2πf). Rotating the coil faster or increasing the number of turns makes the peak emf larger.

cards.h: AC: frequency, peak, and rms value
cards.p: The voltage at an outlet varies as V = Vmax·sin(2πft). The frequency is 50 Hz in Europe and most of the world, and 60 Hz in the Americas. The rms value is Vmax/√2. The 230 V at an outlet is the rms value, and the peak value is about 325 V.
cards.key: The rms value is the DC value that heats a resistor to the same extent. The rms value of the current is likewise Imax/√2. The direction of the current changes 100 times a second.

cards.h: Inductor, capacitor, and resonance in AC
cards.p: The opposition of an inductor, XL = 2πfL, increases with frequency, and that of a capacitor, XC = 1/(2πfC), decreases. When XL = XC there is resonance, and the current is greatest.
cards.key: The opposition of a resistor does not depend on frequency. In a series RLC circuit at resonance, Z = R and f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)).

once.soru: You turn the dial of a radio and pick a station. What is being adjusted in the circuit?

secenekler.neden: The circuit comes into resonance at the station's frequency. So the current of that broadcast is the greatest.
Another knob adjusts the loudness.
Picking a station adjusts the frequency, not the voltage.

cards.p: A transformer is two coils on a shared iron core. The AC in the primary produces a changing flux, and an emf forms in the secondary. In the ideal case V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂, and power is conserved.

etk.soru: Explore the parts of a transformer.

noktalar.acik: It is connected to the AC source. Its changing current creates a changing magnetic flux in the core.
It carries the flux between the two coils. To reduce heat loss, it is made of thin, insulated sheets.
The changing flux creates an emf here. Since N₂ > N₁, V₂ > V₁. This is a step-up transformer.
It is connected to the secondary circuit. In an ideal transformer, the power it draws equals the power drawn from the primary.

cards.p: In a real transformer the windings heat up, and eddy currents form in the iron core. Thin, insulated sheets reduce this loss. The efficiency = P₂/P₁ is always less than 100%.

once.soru: Why does a working charger adapter heat up?

secenekler.neden: The resistance of the windings and the eddy currents in the core turn energy into heat.
An adapter steps the voltage down. The heating is caused by the losses.
The reversing of AC does not produce heat by itself. Resistances produce the heat.

cards.p: The heat loss in the line, I²·R, grows with the square of the current. That is why it pays to transmit the same power (P = V·I) at high voltage and small current.

once.soru: You put a glass pot on an induction cooktop. Does it heat up?

secenekler.neden: Glass is not a conductor. So no eddy current forms in glass.
The cooktop heats the conducting base, not glass.
Without eddy currents there is no heating either.

cards.p:
• When the flux (Φ = B·A·cosθ) changes, an emf forms: ε = −N·ΔΦ/Δt.
• The induced current opposes the change.
• For a rod, ε = B·L·v.
• A generator produces AC. The grid is 50 Hz.
• For a transformer, V₁/V₂ = N₁/N₂, and it works only with AC.

quiz.q: The flux through a 50-turn coil drops steadily from 0.04 Wb to 0.01 Wb in 0.1 s. What is the magnitude of the emf in the coil in volts?
Put in order the path electricity takes from the power plant to your home.
ogeler: A transformer steps the voltage up (154-380 kV)
Electricity travels far on a high-voltage line
Near the city the voltage is stepped down
quiz.e: Since the loss in the line is I²·R, the same power is transmitted at high voltage and small current. So the voltage is stepped up at the plant and stepped down by transformers near the city.

quiz.q: Match each device with what it does.
ciftler: Creates eddy currents in the pan
Creates an emf in a battery-free chip
quiz.e: In a generator, a rotating coil converts mechanical energy into electrical energy. A transformer changes an AC voltage through its turns ratio. An induction cooktop creates eddy currents in the base of the pan. A card reader likewise creates an emf in the coil in the card.

quiz.q: The N pole of a magnet is brought down toward a conducting loop lying on a table. Looking at the loop from where the magnet is, in which direction is the induced current?
o: Clockwise. The top face of the loop is S
Counterclockwise. The top face of the loop is N
Clockwise. The top face of the loop is N
quiz.e: The field leaving the N pole enters the loop downward and increases. To oppose this, the current produces a field upward (toward you). When your right thumb points toward you, the fingers curl counterclockwise. So the top face becomes N and repels the magnet.
y: If the top face were S, it would attract the magnet. By Lenz's law, the loop opposes the approach.
Seen from above, a clockwise current produces a downward field. That makes the top face S, not N.
The loop does not have to move for a current to form. A change in the flux through it is enough.

yari-iletkenler.title: Semiconductors and superconductors
yari-iletkenler.summary: Semiconductors from the diode to the chip, and superconductors with zero resistance.

cards.p: In a metal, some electrons are free and carry current easily. In an insulator there are no free electrons. In semiconductors such as silicon and germanium, free electrons are few, and their number changes with conditions.

once.soru: Most phone chips are made of silicon. How does silicon conduct electricity?

secenekler.yazi: A little or a lot, depending
secenekler.neden: Silicon is a semiconductor. Its conductivity changes with temperature, light, and doping.
Silicon has far fewer free electrons than a metal.
Silicon has a small number of free electrons at room temperature. So it conducts a little.

cards.h: Resistance that changes with heat and light
cards.p: When a metal heats up, its atoms vibrate a lot and the resistance increases. When a semiconductor heats up or receives light, electrons are freed and the resistance decreases.

cards.p: The 4 valence electrons of silicon go into bonds. When a little phosphorus (5 electrons) is added, the fifth electron is left free. This material, in which the extra electrons carry the current, is n-type.

cards.p: When p-type and n-type are joined, a depletion region forms at the boundary. When the plus is connected to p, current flows (forward bias). When it is reversed, it does not. This is a diode.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='20' y='60' width='60' height='40' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.14'/><rect x='80' y='60' width='60' height='40' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.14'/><rect x='77.0' y='60' width='6' height='40' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='3 2'/><text x='42' y='85' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>p</text><text x='118' y='85' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>n</text><text x='80' y='40' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>forward: current flows</text><text x='80' y='124' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>+ → p, − → n · barrier thins</text><rect x='180' y='60' width='60' height='40' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.14'/><rect x='240' y='60' width='60' height='40' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.14'/><rect x='223.0' y='60' width='34' height='40' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='3 2'/><text x='202' y='85' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>p</text><text x='278' y='85' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>n</text><text x='240' y='40' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>reverse: no current</text><text x='240' y='124' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>+ → n · barrier thickens</text><path d='M110 164 L110 188 L134 176 Z' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='135' y1='164' x2='135' y2='188' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='80' y1='176' x2='110' y2='176' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='135' y1='176' x2='165' y2='176' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='176' y='180' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>diode symbol</text></svg>
cards.key: A silicon diode starts to conduct at about 0.7 V. This is how chargers turn alternating current into direct current.

etk.soru: Does the lamp light up? Put each connection in the right group (silicon diode, lamp in series).
ogeler: In reverse the barrier thickens, and no current flows.
The voltage is large, but the direction is reversed. The diode does not conduct.
Forward, but less than 0.7 V: the barrier cannot be overcome.

cards.h: LED: a diode that gives light
cards.p: In a forward-biased LED, electrons combine with holes and give off the energy as light. As the energy gap grows, the light shifts from red to blue.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='20' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>A larger energy gap gives light of higher energy</text><rect x='30' y='103' width='70' height='57' rx='4' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.18' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M50 97 v-20 a15 15 0 0 1 30 0 v20 z' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='65' y='152' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>1.9 eV</text><text x='65' y='178' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>red</text><text x='65' y='194' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>≈ 650 nm</text><rect x='125' y='91' width='70' height='69' rx='4' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.18' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M145 85 v-20 a15 15 0 0 1 30 0 v20 z' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='160' y='152' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>2.3 eV</text><text x='160' y='178' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>green</text><text x='160' y='194' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>≈ 540 nm</text><rect x='220' y='79' width='70' height='81' rx='4' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.18' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M240 73 v-20 a15 15 0 0 1 30 0 v20 z' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='255' y='152' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>2.7 eV</text><text x='255' y='178' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>blue</text><text x='255' y='194' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>≈ 460 nm</text></svg>
cards.key: The blue LED won a Nobel Prize in 2014. An LED gives the light of an incandescent bulb with about one fifth of the energy.

cards.p: A solar cell is a wide p-n junction. Light creates electron-hole pairs. The electric field of the junction separates them, and a direct current flows in the circuit.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='yari-7' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--c4)'/></marker></defs><circle cx='34' cy='34' r='16' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.7'/><path d='M56 44 L120 92' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#yari-7)'/><rect x='40' y='96' width='200' height='30' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.16' stroke='var(--c1)'/><rect x='40' y='126' width='200' height='44' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='48' y='116' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>n</text><text x='48' y='154' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>p</text><circle cx='130' cy='110' r='5' fill='var(--c1)'/><circle cx='130' cy='150' r='6' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='140' y='114' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>electron</text><text x='140' y='154' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>hole</text><path d='M240 104 H290 V82' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M240 160 H290 V114' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='290' cy='98' r='15' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.55' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='160' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>light → electron-hole pair → current</text></svg>
cards.key: The efficiency of silicon panels is about 20-23%. The rest of the light turns into heat or is reflected.

cards.p: A transistor controls a large current with a small signal. It can amplify the current or switch it on and off like a switch. In a classic transistor the signal is the base current. In the transistors in chips (MOSFETs), the signal is the gate voltage.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><circle cx='90' cy='96' r='34' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.6'/><line x1='80' y1='76' x2='80' y2='116' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3.5'/><line x1='80' y1='86' x2='104' y2='66' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='80' y1='106' x2='104' y2='126' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='20' y1='96' x2='80' y2='96' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M104 66 V30' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='8'/><path d='M104 126 V170' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='8'/><text x='4' y='114' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>small current</text><text x='114' y='40' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>large current</text><rect x='180' y='30' width='126' height='64' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='243' y='50' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>amplifier</text><path d='M192 76 q6 -6 12 0 t12 0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M232 76 l8 0' stroke='var(--muted)'/><path d='M246 76 q8 -14 16 0 t16 0 t16 0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='180' y='106' width='126' height='64' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='243' y='126' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>switch</text><text x='243' y='154' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>off 0 · on 1</text></svg>
cards.key: The 0 and 1 in a computer are these on and off states. The tens of billions of transistors in a phone processor are MOSFETs driven by a gate voltage.

cards.p: Processors, memory, camera sensors, LED displays, and solar panels are semiconductors. That is why chip manufacturing is strategic.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='14' y='30' width='92' height='56' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='60' y='63' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>processor</text><rect x='114' y='30' width='92' height='56' rx='6' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='160' y='63' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>memory</text><rect x='214' y='30' width='92' height='56' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='260' y='63' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>camera</text><rect x='14' y='100' width='92' height='56' rx='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='60' y='133' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>display LEDs</text><rect x='114' y='100' width='92' height='56' rx='6' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='160' y='133' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>solar panel</text><rect x='214' y='100' width='92' height='56' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='260' y='133' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>electric car</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>all silicon or another semiconductor</text></svg>
cards.key: The chip shortage of 2021 stopped many car factories for weeks.

once.soru: What is the very pure silicon in chips obtained from?

secenekler.neden: The silicon dioxide in sand is refined and turned into extremely pure silicon.
Steel is made from iron ore, not silicon.
Fuel and plastics are obtained from petroleum.

cards.p: In 1911, when mercury was cooled below 4.2 K, its resistance suddenly became zero. This is called superconductivity. This limiting temperature is called the critical temperature.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><line x1='40' y1='160' x2='300' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='40' y1='30' x2='40' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)'/><path d='M300 50 L130 96 L130 160 L44 160' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M300 60 L50 124' fill='none' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2.4' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><text x='136' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>4.2 K</text><line x1='130' y1='160' x2='130' y2='172' stroke='var(--c2)'/><line x1='56' y1='40' x2='80' y2='40' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='56' y1='58' x2='80' y2='58' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2.4' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><text x='86' y='44' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>mercury: resistance exactly zero at 4.2 K</text><text x='86' y='62' font-size='11' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>ordinary metal: never zero</text><text x='300' y='186' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>temperature →</text><text x='160' y='20' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Onnes, 1911: critical temperature</text></svg>
cards.key: The resistance is exactly zero, but within certain limits. If the temperature exceeds the critical temperature, the magnetic field the critical field, or the current the critical current, superconductivity breaks down.

cards.p: A superconductor pushes the magnetic field out of its interior. This is called the Meissner effect. That is why a magnet lowered over it stays suspended in the air.

cards.key: A magnet floating in the air is the best-known demonstration of superconductivity.

once.soru: What do you look for to prove that a material is a superconductor?

secenekler.neden: Both properties are needed together. Low resistance alone can also appear for other reasons.
A measurement error can also show a resistance near zero. That is why field expulsion is looked for too.
Not every material that is cooled becomes a superconductor.

cards.p: The ceramic YBCO, found in 1987, is a superconductor below 92 K. That is enough for cooling with cheap liquid nitrogen (77 K).
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><line x1='40' y1='100' x2='300' y2='100' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='44' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--c2)'/><line x1='44' y1='95' x2='44' y2='70' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='43.64' y='62' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>Hg 4.2 K</text><text x='43.64' y='46' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>1911</text><circle cx='107' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--c1)'/><line x1='107' y1='105' x2='107' y2='130' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='106.73333333333333' y='144' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>liquid nitrogen 77 K</text><text x='106.73333333333333' y='160' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>cheap coolant</text><circle cx='120' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--c3)'/><line x1='120' y1='95' x2='120' y2='70' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='119.73333333333333' y='62' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>YBCO ≈ 92 K</text><text x='119.73333333333333' y='46' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>1987</text><circle cx='294' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--muted)'/><line x1='294' y1='105' x2='294' y2='130' stroke='var(--muted)'/><text x='293.93333333333334' y='144' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>room 293 K</text><text x='293.93333333333334' y='160' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>none yet</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>above 77 K, liquid nitrogen is enough</text></svg>
cards.key: There is still no superconductor that works at room temperature. The biggest obstacle is the cost of cooling.

cards.p: The powerful magnets of MRI machines are superconducting coils. A superconducting maglev train reached 603 km/h in 2015.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='14' y='40' width='92' height='100' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='60' y='84' font-size='15' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>MRI</text><text x='60' y='110' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>strong magnet</text><rect x='114' y='40' width='92' height='100' rx='6' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='160' y='84' font-size='15' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>maglev</text><text x='160' y='110' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>603 km/h (2015)</text><rect x='214' y='40' width='92' height='100' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='260' y='84' font-size='15' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>CERN</text><text x='260' y='110' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>magnets at 1.9 K</text><text x='160' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>zero resistance: large current, no heating</text><text x='160' y='20' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Cooling is costly, but the gain is large</text></svg>
cards.key: Zero resistance means a very large current and a very strong field without heating, up to the critical current. CERN's magnets and many quantum computers are superconducting too.

once.soru: Why are the coils of a hospital MRI machine cooled with liquid helium?

secenekler.neden: The resistance of the cold coil is zero. The coil carries a very large current without heating and produces a strong field.

secenekler.yazi: To keep the magnet from melting
secenekler.neden: The coil does not heat anywhere near melting. The aim of the cooling is to bring the resistance to zero.
A strong magnetic field gives the image. That field is produced by the superconducting coil.

cards.p:
• The conductivity of a semiconductor changes with temperature, light, and doping.
• Electrons carry the current in n-type, and holes in p-type.
• A diode passes current in one direction.
• An LED gives light, and a solar cell produces current.
• A transistor controls a large current.
• The resistance of a superconductor is zero.

quiz.q: Put each application in a group by the material it relies on.
quiz.e: LEDs, solar panels, processors, and thermistors work with a p-n junction or a doped semiconductor. MRI, maglev, and accelerator magnets produce very strong fields with zero-resistance superconducting coils.

quiz.q: Match the concepts with their jobs.
ciftler: Controls a large current with a small signal
quiz.e: Phosphorus doping brings extra electrons, and boron doping brings holes. Joining p and n makes a diode. In a transistor, a small signal (base current or gate voltage) switches a large current on and off.

quiz.q: Put the events in a solar cell in order (the first one at the top).
ogeler: A photon is absorbed at the junction
The junction field pushes the electron to n and the hole to p
Current flows in the external circuit
quiz.e: Light first frees an electron, and a hole is left behind. The electric field of the junction separates the two. The separated charges travel around the external circuit and make a current.

quiz.q: The resistance of a material increases when it is cooled and decreases when it is heated. Which is this material most likely to be?
quiz.e: When a semiconductor heats up, more electrons are freed and its resistance decreases. In metals the opposite happens.
y: When a metal heats up, its atoms vibrate more and the resistance increases.
Below the critical temperature, the resistance of YBCO is exactly zero and does not change.
Silver is also a metal, and its resistance increases when it heats up.

optik.title: Optics
optik.summary: Shadows, reflection, mirrors, refraction, lenses, colors, and the eye.

cards.h: Light travels in straight lines: shadows
cards.p: Light travels along straight lines. That is why a shadow forms behind an opaque obstacle. A point source makes a full shadow (umbra). An extended source also makes a partial shadow (penumbra) around it.

cards.key: No light from any point of the source reaches the umbra, and light from part of the source reaches the penumbra. This is how eclipses happen.

cards.p: As light moves away from the source it spreads over a larger area, and the illuminance decreases: E = I·cosθ/d². When the distance doubles, the illuminance drops to one quarter.

cards.key: I is the luminous intensity, and its unit is the candela. θ is the angle between the ray and the normal. The unit of luminous flux is the lumen, and the unit of illuminance is the lux (lumen/m²).

once.soru: If you move a desk lamp twice as far from a book, how well is the book lit?

secenekler.neden: The same light spreads over 4 times the area. So illuminance decreases with the square of the distance.
The distance doubles, but the area the light spreads over grows 4 times.
Light spreads over a larger area as it moves away.

cards.p: In reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The angles are measured from the normal, the line perpendicular to the surface. A smooth surface gives specular reflection, and a rough surface gives diffuse reflection.

cards.p: The image in a plane mirror is virtual, upright, and the same size as the object. The image forms behind the mirror, at the same distance as the object. If the mirror is rotated by α, the reflected ray rotates by 2α.

cards.p: In a spherical mirror, the center of curvature is shown with C and the focus with F, and f = r/2. A concave mirror converges light. The image forms where two special reflected rays cross.

etk.soru: Explore the key points of a concave mirror.

noktalar.acik: This is the axis of symmetry that passes through the vertex of the mirror and the center of curvature.
This is the center of the sphere the mirror is part of. A ray coming through C returns along itself.
Rays coming parallel to the axis pass through here after reflecting. f = r / 2.
This is the point where the mirror meets the principal axis. f and r are measured from here.
In a concave mirror the reflecting face is on the inside. That is why the mirror converges light.

once.soru: You can gather sunlight at one point with a concave mirror and burn paper. What is that point called?

secenekler.neden: Rays coming in parallel gather at the focus after reflecting.
The center of curvature is twice as far as the focus. The rays do not gather there.
The vertex is a point on the mirror. The rays gather in front of the mirror.

cards.p: In a concave mirror, if the object is outside F the image is real and inverted. If the object is between F and the mirror, the image is virtual, upright, and enlarged. A convex mirror always gives a virtual, upright, and reduced image.

cards.p: When light passes into another medium at an angle, it bends because its speed changes. The refractive index is n = c/v, and it is 1.33 for water. According to Snell's law, n₁·sinθ₁ = n₂·sinθ₂. In the medium with the larger index, the ray bends toward the normal.

cards.key: Optical density is not mass density. For example, oil is lighter than water, but its refractive index is larger.

cards.h: Total internal reflection and the critical angle
cards.p: Light passing from a medium with a larger index into one with a smaller index bends away from the normal. When the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, the light cannot get out and is reflected back completely. This is called total internal reflection.

cards.p: Light from an object in water bends away from the normal as it comes out into air. Since the eye extends the rays straight back, it sees the object higher than it is. That is why a pool looks shallower than it is.

once.soru: You look from above at a coin on the bottom of a pool. Where does the coin appear?

secenekler.neden: Light bends as it leaves the water. The eye extends it straight back and sees the coin higher up.
Since light bends at the water surface, the coin appears displaced.
Refraction makes the coin look raised.

cards.p: A lens with thin edges converges light and is called a converging lens. A lens with thick edges spreads light and is called a diverging lens. A ray coming parallel to the axis passes through the focus. A ray through the center is not deviated.

once.soru: You can gather sunlight at one point with a magnifying glass. What are the edges of a magnifying glass like?

secenekler.neden: A lens that is thick in the middle and thin at the edges converges light.
A lens with thick edges spreads light.
Flat glass does not converge light.

cards.p: For mirrors and lenses, 1/f = 1/do + 1/di. The magnification is found with m = −di/do. If m is negative the image is inverted, and if it is positive the image is upright.

etk.soru: A concave mirror or converging lens (f > 0). Move the object closer and farther. Where is the image?
yorum: The image is virtual, upright, and enlarged. The object is between F and the mirror (lens).
The image is real and inverted. The object is outside F.

once.soru: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di. For a concave mirror, f = 10 cm and the object is 15 cm away. How many cm away is the image?

secenekler.neden: Distances are not added. You take the difference of their reciprocals: 1/10 − 1/15.
The result is not 15 − 10. 1/di = 1/10 − 1/15 = 1/30.

cards.h: Calculations for convex mirrors and diverging lenses
cards.p: For a convex mirror and a diverging lens, f is negative. If f = −10 cm and the object is 15 cm away, then d<sub>i</sub> = −6 cm. This image is virtual, upright, and reduced.

once.soru: A car's side mirror says "Objects in mirror are closer than they appear". Why?

secenekler.neden: A convex mirror gives a virtual and reduced image. So a vehicle looks farther away than it is.
The warning is because of the shape of the mirror.
If it enlarged them, objects would look closer.

cards.p: The refractive index of glass changes with color. That is why white light splits into its colors in a prism. Red bends the least, and violet the most. A rainbow forms by refraction and reflection in raindrops.

once.soru: Where must the Sun be for you to see a rainbow?

secenekler.neden: Light refracts and reflects in the drops in front of you and comes back to you.
When you face the Sun, the light reflected from the drops does not reach you.
When the Sun is very high, the rainbow stays below the horizon.

cards.h: Colors in light and in paint
cards.p: The primary colors of light are red, green, and blue. When the three combine, white light forms. An object appears in the color it reflects from the light that falls on it. A filter lets only its own color through.

cards.key: In paint the primary colors are cyan, magenta, and yellow. A red apple looks black in blue light.

cards.p: The eye is like a converging lens, and a real, inverted, and reduced image forms on the retina. A nearsighted person cannot see far objects clearly and uses a diverging lens. A farsighted person cannot see near objects clearly and uses a converging lens.

cards.p:
• In reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
• A plane mirror gives a virtual, upright image of the same size.
• n₁·sinθ₁ = n₂·sinθ₂.
• Beyond the critical angle there is total internal reflection.
• For mirrors and lenses, 1/f = 1/do + 1/di.
• Nearsighted eyes get a diverging lens, farsighted eyes a converging lens.

quiz.q: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a converging lens with a focal length of 20 cm. How many cm from the lens does the image form?
quiz.e: 1/d<sub>i</sub> = 1/20 − 1/30 = 1/60, so d<sub>i</sub> = +60 cm. Since this value is positive, the image is real and inverted. The magnification is m = −60/30 = −2.

quiz.q: Is the image in each case real or virtual? Put it in the right group.
quiz.e: In a concave mirror, if the object is outside F the image is real and inverted. The image on the retina is real too. A plane mirror, a convex mirror, and a diverging lens give virtual images. In a concave mirror, the image of an object between F and the mirror is also virtual.

quiz.q: Match each case with the related optical principle or device.
quiz.e: In a nearsighted eye the image falls in front of the retina, and a diverging lens is used. In a farsighted eye the image falls behind the retina, and a converging lens is used. A convex mirror gives a wide field of view. Fiber optics relies on total internal reflection. A pool looks shallow because light bends as it passes from water into air.

quiz.q: Light traveling inside glass with a refractive index of 1.5 toward air strikes the glass-air surface at an angle of incidence of 45°. What happens? (sin 45° ≈ 0.71)
o: It passes into air, bending toward the normal
It passes into air without bending or changing direction
The angle of refraction is 90°, and it skims the surface
It cannot pass into air and is totally reflected
quiz.e: For the critical angle, sin θc = 1/1.5 ≈ 0.67, so θc ≈ 42°. Since the angle of incidence, 45°, is larger than this, the light undergoes total internal reflection.
y: Light passing from a larger index to a smaller index bends away from the normal. What is more, the critical angle is exceeded here.
Light keeps its direction only if it arrives along the normal. Light arriving at 45° is either refracted or reflected.
The angle of refraction is 90° only when the angle of incidence equals the critical angle. sin 45° ≈ 0.71 is larger than 0.67. So 45° is larger than θc ≈ 42°.

dalga-optigi.title: Interference and diffraction of light
dalga-optigi.summary: Learn about Young's experiment, fringe spacing, single-slit diffraction, and polarization.

cards.p: According to Huygens, every point of a wavefront is a source that sends out small wavelets. The common tangent of these wavelets forms the new wavefront. This principle explains diffraction and refraction.

cards.h: Young's experiment: light is a wave
cards.p: In 1801 Young passed light of a single color through two narrow slits. On the screen he saw bright and dark fringes. Darkness forming where light falls on light can only be explained by the interference of waves.

cards.key: Newton thought light was a stream of particles, and Huygens thought it was a wave. The double-slit pattern shows most clearly that light behaves like a wave.

once.soru: If you pass single-color light through two narrow slits onto a screen, what do you see?

secenekler.neden: The waves from the two slits interfere. So bright and dark fringes form in turn.
That would happen if light were only particles. But the experiment shows an interference pattern.
The waves cancel each other at some points. That is why dark bands form.

cards.p: The two slits behave like two sources in phase. The path difference of the rays reaching point P is Δ = |r2 − r1|. If the screen is far away, Δ ≈ d·sinθ.

cards.key: θ is the angle between the direction of the center and the direction of P. Whether P is bright or dark is decided by the ratio of Δ to λ.

once.soru: Point P is 5.0 µm from S₁ and 6.2 µm from S₂. What is the path difference?

secenekler.neden: The path difference is the difference of the two distances: 6.2 − 5.0.
The distances are subtracted, not added.
That is only the distance to S₂. You have to take the difference of the two distances.

cards.h: Conditions for bright and dark fringes
cards.p: If the path difference is a whole multiple of λ (Δ = n·λ), there is constructive interference and a bright fringe forms. If it is a half multiple (Δ = (n − ½)·λ), there is destructive interference and a dark fringe forms.
cards.key: For example, if Δ = 2λ, this is the 2nd bright fringe. If Δ = 2.5λ, this is the 3rd dark fringe.

cards.h: Distance of the fringes from the center
cards.p: At the center the path difference is zero, and the central bright fringe forms there. At a distance x from the center, Δ ≈ d·x/L. The nth bright fringe is at a distance x = n·λL/d from the center.
cards.key: The nth dark fringe is at a distance x = (n − ½)·λL/d from the center. The pattern is symmetric about the center.

cards.p: The distance between two neighboring bright fringes is called the fringe spacing: Δx = λ·L/d. If λ or L increases the fringes spread apart, and if d increases they get closer. The intensity of the light does not change Δx.

cards.key: In red light the fringes are wider than in violet, because red has a longer wavelength.

etk.soru: Change the wavelength, the screen distance, and the slit separation: Δx = λL/d.

cards.p: Let λ = 450 nm, d = 0.25 mm, and L = 1 m. Then Δx = 1.8 mm. The 2nd bright fringe is 3.6 mm away, and the 1st dark fringe is 0.9 mm away.

cards.key: Δx = (4.5×10⁻⁷ · 1) / (2.5×10⁻⁴) m. A common mistake is to calculate without converting nm to 10⁻⁹ m and mm to 10⁻³ m.

once.soru: λ = 450 nm, d = 0.25 mm, L = 1 m. What is the fringe spacing Δx = λL/d in mm?

secenekler.neden: When you convert the units to meters, the result comes out 10 times smaller.
1 nm is 10⁻⁹ m, and 1 mm is 10⁻³ m. The result is 1.8×10⁻³ m.

cards.h: If the setup is put under water
cards.p: When the setup is immersed in a liquid of refractive index n, the frequency does not change. The wavelength becomes n times smaller: λ′ = λ/n. The fringe spacing gets smaller too: Δx′ = Δx/n.

cards.h: Where does the central fringe shift?
cards.p: If a thin transparent plate is placed in front of one of the slits, the light on that path is delayed. In this case the central fringe shifts toward the plate. If the source is moved, the central fringe shifts the opposite way.

cards.key: In both cases the fringe spacing does not change. The whole pattern shifts together.

once.soru: A thin piece of glass is placed in front of the upper slit. Where does the central bright fringe shift?

secenekler.neden: The glass delays the light on the upper path. So the point where the two beams meet with equal delay shifts toward the glass.
Since the delay is on the upper path, the balance point shifts to the upper side.
Since the glass delays the light on one path, the point of zero path difference changes.

cards.p: In white light, each color forms its own pattern. At the center the path difference is zero for all colors. That is why the central fringe is white. The inner edge of the side fringes is violet, and the outer edge is red.
cards.key: Violet light has the shortest wavelength, so its fringes are closest to the center. Farther from the center, the colors mix.

once.soru: If Young's experiment is done with white light, what color is the central fringe?

secenekler.neden: At the center all colors interfere constructively and combine into white.
Violet fringes are closest to the center, but all colors meet at the center.
Red fringes are farthest from the center.

cards.p: Light passing through a single narrow slit also forms a pattern. For a slit of width w, the condition for a dark fringe is w·sinθ = n·λ. The central fringe is twice as wide as the side fringes.
cards.key: The width of a side fringe is λL/w. For a dark fringe in a single slit you write n·λ. Do not confuse this with (n − ½)·λ for the double slit.

cards.p: In a double slit the fringes are equally wide and similar in brightness. In a single slit the central fringe is wide and bright, and the sides are faint. As the slit gets narrower, the pattern widens.

once.soru: On the screen there is a pattern with a very wide, bright middle and faint sides. What did the light pass through?

secenekler.neden: In a single slit the central fringe is twice as wide, and the sides fade quickly.
In a double slit the fringes are about equal in width and brightness.
A prism splits light into its colors, but it does not form a bright-dark pattern.

cards.p: In a soap bubble or a thin layer of oil on water, part of the light reflects from the top surface of the film and part from the bottom surface. These two rays interfere, and the film looks colored.

cards.key: The thickness of the film and the viewing angle decide which color gets stronger. A very thin soap film looks dark, because one of the reflected rays is shifted by half a wave.

once.soru: Why does a soap bubble look colored?

secenekler.neden: The rays reflected from the two surfaces of the film strengthen some colors and cancel others.
Colorless soap also makes colored bubbles.
The colors come from interference, not from absorption.

cards.h: Polarization: light is a transverse wave
cards.p: What vibrates in light is the electric field. A polarizer lets through only the vibration in a single direction. Only transverse waves can be polarized. Light is a transverse wave, and sound cannot be polarized.

cards.p:
• Young's experiment shows that light is a wave.
• For bright fringes Δ = n·λ, and for dark fringes Δ = (n − ½)·λ.
• The fringe spacing is Δx = λL/d and drops to Δx/n in a liquid.
• In a single slit the central fringe is 2 times as wide.
• Polarization proves that light is a transverse wave.

quiz.q: In Young's experiment, λ = 500 nm, the slit separation is d = 0.25 mm, and the screen distance is L = 2 m. How many mm is it from the central bright fringe to the 3rd bright fringe?
quiz.e: Δx = λL/d = (5×10<sup>−7</sup> · 2)/(2.5×10<sup>−4</sup>) = 4×10<sup>−3</sup> m = 4 mm. The 3rd bright fringe is 3·Δx = 12 mm from the center.

quiz.q: In the double-slit experiment, match the path difference (Δ) at point P with the fringe observed.
quiz.e: For a bright fringe Δ = n·λ, and for a dark fringe Δ = (n − ½)·λ. So 0.5λ is the n = 1 dark fringe, and 1.5λ is the n = 2 dark fringe.

quiz.q: How does each change affect the fringe spacing (Δx = λL/d) in Young's experiment? (λ: wavelength, L: screen distance, d: slit separation)
quiz.e: Δx is directly proportional to λ and L, and inversely proportional to d. In water the wavelength is λ/n, so Δx is divided by n too. The intensity of the light only makes the fringes brighter and does not change the spacing.

quiz.q: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, if the slit is made narrower, what can be said about the central bright fringe?
quiz.e: The width of the central fringe is 2λL/w. When w gets smaller, this width increases. Diffraction becomes more pronounced as the slit approaches the wavelength.
y: The width of the central fringe is 2λL/w. As the slit narrows, the light spreads more and the fringe widens.
The fringe width depends on the width of the slit. When w gets smaller, 2λL/w grows and the fringe widens.
All the wavelets reach the center in phase. So a bright fringe always forms there, and the fringe only widens.

ozel-gorelilik.title: Special relativity
ozel-gorelilik.summary: Learn why the speed of light is constant, and meet time dilation, length contraction and E = mc².

cards.p: In classical physics, velocities add. A ball thrown at 20 m/s relative to a train moving at 30 m/s travels at 50 m/s relative to the ground. With light, measurements always give c.

cards.h: The ether and the Michelson–Morley experiment
cards.p: In the 19th century, light was thought to travel through a medium called the ether. In 1887 Michelson and Morley looked for a difference in the speed of light with direction. They found no difference, and the ether was never found.

cards.p: In 1905 Einstein put forward two postulates. First, the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. Second, the speed of light in a vacuum is c ≈ 3·108 m/s for everyone.

cards.p: The time measured in the frame where the events happen at the same place is called proper time (Δt0). A moving observer measures a longer time: Δt = γ·Δt0. Here γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).

etk.soru: Change the speed of the ship. While the clock on the ship measures Δt<sub>0</sub>, what does the clock on Earth measure?

cards.h: The γ factor and everyday speeds
cards.p: γ is never less than 1. For a jet flying at 300 m/s, γ ≈ 1 + 5·10<sup>−13</sup>, a difference only an atomic clock can measure. As the speed gets close to c, γ grows quickly.
cards.key: At everyday speeds γ ≈ 1 and relativity turns into Newtonian physics.

cards.p: The length of an object measured in its own frame is called its proper length (L0). A moving observer measures it shorter: L = L0/γ. The contraction happens only along the direction of motion.
