cards.h: Relativistic momentum and the c limit
cards.p: At high speeds momentum is p = γ·m·v. As v gets close to c, γ and the energy needed grow without limit. That is why no object with mass can reach c.
cards.key: Only massless particles such as the photon move at c.

cards.p: Even an object at rest has rest energy: E0 = m·c². A mass of 1 g corresponds to 9·1013 J of energy. The mass Δm lost in fission and fusion is released as an energy of Δm·c².
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='40' font-size='24' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>E₀ = m·c²</text><text x='10' y='92' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>reactants</text><rect x='80' y='78' width='220' height='22' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5' rx='3'/><text x='10' y='132' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>products</text><rect x='80' y='118' width='196' height='22' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5' rx='3'/><rect x='276' y='118' width='24' height='22' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='3 2'/><text x='288' y='158' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Δm</text><text x='80' y='158' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>(difference exaggerated)</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>lost mass → energy E = Δm·c²</text></svg>
cards.key: Fission is the splitting of a nucleus, and fusion is the joining of nuclei. You will see binding energy and mass defect in the topic “The atomic nucleus and radioactivity”.

once.soru: With E = m·c², how many joules is 1 g of mass? (c = 3·10⁸ m/s)

secenekler.neden: c must be squared: (3·10⁸)² = 9·10¹⁶.
This value is for 1 kg. 1 g is one thousandth of it.

cards.p: The total energy of a moving object is E = γ·m·c², and its kinetic energy is Ek = (γ − 1)·m·c². At low speed this reduces to ½mv². Mass does not grow with speed; what grows is γ.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='28' font-size='17' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>E = γ·m·c²</text><text x='160' y='50' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>E<tspan dy='3' font-size='10'>k</tspan><tspan dy='-3'> = (γ − 1)·m·c²</tspan></text><text x='10' y='92' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>0.6c</text><rect x='50' y='78' width='160' height='22' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5' rx='3'/><rect x='210' y='78' width='40' height='22' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5' rx='3'/><text x='130' y='94' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>m·c²</text><text x='256' y='94' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>0.25 m·c²</text><text x='10' y='136' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>0.8c</text><rect x='50' y='122' width='160' height='22' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5' rx='3'/><rect x='210' y='122' width='106.7' height='22' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5' rx='3'/><text x='130' y='138' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>m·c²</text><text x='263' y='138' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>0.67 m·c²</text><text x='130' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>rest energy</text><text x='263' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>kinetic energy</text><text x='160' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>m does not change; γ grows</text></svg>
cards.key: The relativistic mass γ·m found in some books is really γ entering momentum and energy. Mass (m) is constant.

once.soru: For an object moving at 0.6c, γ = 1.25. What fraction of m·c² is its kinetic energy?

secenekler.neden: That is the total energy. The rest energy must be subtracted.

cards.p: The clocks on GPS satellites fall behind by about 7 μs a day because of their speed. Because of the weaker gravity they run ahead by about 45 μs a day. Without this correction, the position error would grow by about 10 km a day.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='50' cy='160' r='85' fill='none' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><circle cx='50' cy='160' r='38' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='50' y='165' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>Earth</text><rect x='86.5' y='80.4' width='12' height='12' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='76.5' y1='86.4' x2='85.5' y2='86.4' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><line x1='99.5' y1='86.4' x2='108.5' y2='86.4' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><text x='92.5' y='72.4' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>satellite</text><text x='165' y='28' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>Satellite clock, per day:</text><text x='165' y='54' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)'>special (speed): −7 μs</text><text x='165' y='76' font-size='12' fill='var(--c5)'>general (gravity): +45 μs</text><line x1='165' y1='88' x2='305' y2='88' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1' fill='none'/><text x='165' y='106' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='bold'>net: ≈ +38 μs ahead</text><text x='165' y='140' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>without correction</text><text x='165' y='160' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>≈ 10 km/day error</text></svg>
cards.key: The satellites orbit at a height of ≈20 200 km at ≈3.9 km/s. GPS applies both the special (speed) and the general (gravity) relativity correction.

once.soru: Is relativity taken into account so that the GPS in your phone works correctly?

secenekler.neden: Clock differences of microseconds cause position errors of kilometers.
The difference is small, but multiplied by the speed of light it reaches kilometers.
The satellite clocks are corrected for every user.

cards.p:
• Everyone measures the speed of light as c, and there is no ether.
• Simultaneity is relative.
• Time dilates: Δt = γ·Δt0.
• Length contracts along the motion: L = L0/γ.
• An object with mass cannot reach c, and E0 = m·c².
• When v ≪ c, γ ≈ 1.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='10' width='300' height='32' fill='var(--panel)' rx='6'/><text x='24' y='31' font-size='13' fill='var(--acc)' font-weight='bold'>γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²)</text><text x='296' y='31' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>always ≥ 1</text><rect x='10' y='47' width='300' height='32' fill='var(--panel)' rx='6'/><text x='24' y='68' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' font-weight='bold'>Δt = γ·Δt₀</text><text x='296' y='68' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>time dilates</text><rect x='10' y='84' width='300' height='32' fill='var(--panel)' rx='6'/><text x='24' y='105' font-size='13' fill='var(--c5)' font-weight='bold'>L = L₀/γ</text><text x='296' y='105' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>length contracts</text><rect x='10' y='121' width='300' height='32' fill='var(--panel)' rx='6'/><text x='24' y='142' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>p = γ·m·v</text><text x='296' y='142' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>v < c</text><rect x='10' y='158' width='300' height='32' fill='var(--panel)' rx='6'/><text x='24' y='179' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>E₀ = m·c²</text><text x='296' y='179' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>rest energy</text></svg>

quiz.q: On a ship moving at 0.6c relative to Earth, 12 years pass by the ship's clock. How many years pass for an observer on Earth?
quiz.e: At 0.6c, γ = 1/√(1 − 0.36) = 1.25. The time on the ship is the proper time. So Δt = 1.25·12 = 15 years.

quiz.q: For two observers moving at constant velocity relative to each other, put each quantity in the right group.
ogeler: Speed of light in a vacuum
quiz.e: By Einstein's postulates, the laws of physics and the speed of light in a vacuum are the same for everyone. Simultaneity, time intervals and length along the direction of motion depend on the observer. Length perpendicular to the motion does not contract.

quiz.q: Match each concept with its example.
ciftler: A muon's lifetime is measured longer from the ground
A fast ship is measured shorter from the ground
quiz.e: Because the muon moves fast, its lifetime is measured γ times longer from the ground. A fast ship is measured γ times shorter along its motion. By E<sub>0</sub> = m·c², 1 g of mass equals 9·10<sup>13</sup> J. Michelson and Morley did not see the expected shift.

quiz.q: Which is true for an astronaut on a ship moving very fast relative to Earth?
o: They notice their own clock running slow.
They see the things on the ship as contracted.
They can exceed c by running the engines long enough.
They see their own clock running normally.
quiz.e: The astronaut is at rest in their own frame, and everything there runs normally. Time dilation and length contraction show up in the measurements of an observer moving relative to the ship.
y: The astronaut sees their own clock running normally. It is the observer on Earth who measures the clock as slow.
For the astronaut, the ship and the things on it are at rest. Only the observer on Earth measures the contraction.
As an object with mass speeds up, the energy needed goes to infinity. So the object cannot reach the speed of light or exceed it.

kuantum.title: Introduction to quantum physics
kuantum.summary: Blackbody, photon, photoelectric effect, Compton, de Broglie and the Bohr model.

cards.p: Every object radiates. An ideal object that absorbs all the light falling on it is called a blackbody. As temperature rises, the radiation grows and the peak wavelength gets shorter: λmax·T ≈ 2.9×10⁻³ m·K.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='kuant-1' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><path d='M40 30 V170 H300' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M44 168 C68 160, 80 52, 104 52 C132 52, 165 135, 296 162' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M48 169 C95 166, 122 112, 160 112 C196 112, 230 150, 296 165' fill='none' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M104 54 V170 M160 114 V170' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='86' y='50' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>T₂</text><text x='168' y='142' font-size='13' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>T₁</text><text x='104' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>λ₂</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='middle'>λ₁</text><path d='M150 140 H116' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#kuant-1)'/><text x='300' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>λ</text><text x='46' y='26' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>intensity</text><text x='300' y='60' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>T₂ > T₁</text><text x='300' y='78' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>hotter: the peak moves</text><text x='300' y='92' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>to shorter wavelengths</text><text x='230' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>λ<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>max</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan>·T ≈ 2.9×10⁻³ m·K</text></svg>
cards.key: Every object above absolute zero radiates. Heated iron glows red first, then close to white. The Sun radiates in the visible, and you radiate in the infrared.

cards.p: Classical physics predicted that radiation would grow without limit at short wavelengths. But the experiments did not show this. In 1900 Planck proposed that energy is exchanged in packets called quanta: E = n·h·f.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='kuant-2' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><path d='M20 40 V160 H150' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M42 42 C50 110, 80 140, 148 150' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5 3'/><path d='M24 159 C40 150, 52 90, 70 90 C90 90, 105 140, 148 153' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='56' y='36' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start'>classical prediction</text><text x='96' y='104' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>experiment</text><text x='150' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>λ</text><text x='85' y='194' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>ultraviolet catastrophe</text><path d='M165 30 V180' stroke='var(--line)'/><path d='M180 150 L232 100' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M250 150 H262 V136 H274 V122 H286 V108 H298 V94' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='206' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>continuous</text><text x='274' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>in packets</text><text x='304' y='126' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>h·f</text><text x='240' y='34' font-size='18' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>E = n·h·f</text><text x='240' y='54' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>n = 1, 2, 3, ...</text><text x='240' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>h ≈ 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s</text></svg>
cards.key: h ≈ 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant. Energy can change only by whole multiples of h·f.

once.soru: According to Planck, how does a light source give off energy?

secenekler.neden: Energy is exchanged in packets of size h·f.
Classical physics thought so, but this idea did not agree with experiment.
The source radiates continuously, but its energy changes packet by packet.

cards.p: Light is made of packets called photons. The energy of a photon is E = h·f = h·c/λ. At the atomic scale the unit electronvolt is used: E(eV) ≈ 1240 / λ(nm).
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='kuant-3' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='36' font-size='20' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>E = h·f = h·c / λ</text><rect x='30' y='78' width='52' height='28' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.75'/><rect x='82' y='78' width='52' height='28' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.75'/><rect x='134' y='78' width='52' height='28' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.75'/><rect x='186' y='78' width='52' height='28' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.75'/><rect x='238' y='78' width='52' height='28' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.75'/><text x='30' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>400 nm</text><text x='290' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>700 nm</text><text x='30' y='126' font-size='13' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>≈ 3.1 eV</text><text x='290' y='126' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>≈ 1.8 eV</text><path d='M210 146 H110' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#kuant-3)'/><text x='160' y='162' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>photon energy increases</text><text x='160' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J   ·   E(eV) ≈ 1240 / λ(nm)</text></svg>
cards.key: 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J. The shorter the wavelength, the greater the photon energy.

once.soru: Which photon has more energy?

secenekler.neden: The photon with the shorter wavelength has more energy: 1240/400 ≈ 3.1 eV.
The energy of the red photon is 1240/700 ≈ 1.8 eV.
Photon energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

cards.h: The photoelectric effect and the threshold
cards.p: When light falling on a metal knocks out electrons, this is called the photoelectric effect. The smallest energy needed for this is called the work function: W = h·f0. If f < f0, no electron comes out.
cards.key: f₀ is the threshold frequency, and W is also called the binding energy. Frequency sets the threshold. Intensity or waiting time does not.

cards.p: An electron absorbs a single photon. An amount W of the energy goes into freeing the electron, and the rest becomes kinetic energy: Ek,max = h·f − W. Electrons from deeper in the metal come out slower.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='kuant-5' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='30' font-size='18' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>E<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>k,max</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan> = h·f − W</text><rect x='50' y='55' width='44' height='110' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='150' y='92' width='44' height='73' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='150' y='55' width='44' height='37' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='122' y='115' font-size='18' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>=</text><text x='72' y='184' font-size='12' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>photon: h·f = 3 eV</text><text x='204' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>E<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>k,max</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan> = 1 eV</text><text x='204' y='86' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>the rest: motion</text><text x='204' y='126' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>W = 2 eV</text><text x='204' y='142' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>frees the electron</text><text x='172' y='184' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>electron</text></svg>
cards.key: As f increases, the maximum kinetic energy increases too, but it is not directly proportional to f, because W is subtracted.

etk.soru: Change the wavelength of the light and the work function of the metal. E(eV) ≈ 1240 / λ(nm).
yorum: No electron is ejected, because the photon energy is less than W (f < f<sub>0</sub>). Raising the intensity does not help either.
This is exactly the threshold (f = f<sub>0</sub>), and the photon energy equals W. The electron barely gets out and its kinetic energy is zero.
The electron is ejected, but it comes out very slowly. The photon energy is only slightly above W, and the small extra energy becomes kinetic energy.
The electron is ejected, because the photon energy is greater than W. The extra energy becomes kinetic energy.

cards.p: When intensity rises, more photons arrive each second and more electrons are ejected. So the saturation current rises, but Ek,max does not change. For the stopping voltage, e·V0 = Ek,max.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='kuant-6' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><path d='M20 150 H300' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#kuant-6)'/><path d='M150 178 V30' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#kuant-6)'/><path d='M100 150 C118 110, 150 62, 192 58 L296 58' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M100 150 C118 128, 150 104, 192 102 L296 102' fill='none' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='296' y='50' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>high intensity</text><text x='296' y='94' font-size='11' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>low intensity</text><circle cx='100' cy='150' r='3' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='100' y='168' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>−V<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>0</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan></text><text x='100' y='188' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>same V<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>0</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan></text><text x='300' y='168' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>V</text><text x='158' y='34' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>I</text><text x='20' y='30' font-size='13' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>e·V<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>0</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan> = E<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>k,max</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan></text></svg>
cards.key: Intensity changes the current. V₀ is set only by the frequency of the light and the kind of metal.

cards.p: The graph of Ek,max against frequency is a straight line. Its slope is h, the same for every metal. The line crosses the f axis at the threshold frequency f0.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='kuant-7' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><path d='M40 130 H300' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#kuant-7)'/><path d='M40 192 V22' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#kuant-7)'/><path d='M100 130 L210 38' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M40 180 L100 130' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><path d='M160 130 L270 38' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='216' y='38' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>K</text><text x='276' y='38' font-size='13' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>L</text><text x='100' y='146' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>f<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>0K</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan></text><text x='160' y='146' font-size='12' fill='var(--c5)' text-anchor='middle'>f<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>0L</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan></text><text x='34' y='184' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>−W<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>K</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan></text><text x='48' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>E<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>k,max</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan></text><text x='300' y='146' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>f</text><text x='300' y='98' font-size='13' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>slope = h</text><text x='300' y='114' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>lines are parallel</text><text x='200' y='178' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>W<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>L</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan> > W<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>K</tspan><tspan dy='-3'></tspan></text></svg>
cards.key: Extended backward, the line crosses the vertical axis at −W. The lines for different metals are parallel.

once.soru: The Ek,max–frequency graph is drawn for two different metals. How do the slopes of the lines compare?

secenekler.neden: The slope is Planck's constant h and does not depend on the metal.
W only shifts the line to the right. It does not change the slope.
The slope is h for every metal.

cards.p: In a Compton collision, energy and momentum are conserved. A photon has no mass, but it has momentum: p = h/λ. Since the electron takes energy, the wavelength of the scattered photon gets longer.
cards.key: The Compton effect shows that light collides like a particle.

cards.p: According to de Broglie, every particle has a wavelength: λ = h/(m·v). Electrons sent at a crystal formed a diffraction pattern, just like light. The wavelength of a ball is far too small to measure.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='kuant-9' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='32' font-size='20' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>λ = h / (m·v)</text><rect x='14' y='70' width='36' height='22' rx='3' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--muted)'/><text x='32' y='110' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>electron</text><path d='M52 81 H128' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#kuant-9)'/><rect x='134' y='58' width='12' height='46' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.4' stroke='var(--c4)'/><text x='140' y='122' font-size='11' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='middle'>crystal</text><path d='M146 81 L236 56 M146 81 L236 106 M146 81 L236 81' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1' stroke-opacity='0.5'/><circle cx='270' cy='81' r='6' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3' stroke-opacity='0.9'/><circle cx='270' cy='81' r='15' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3' stroke-opacity='0.6'/><circle cx='270' cy='81' r='24' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3' stroke-opacity='0.4'/><text x='270' y='122' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>diffraction rings</text><path d='M10 140 H310' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='14' y='162' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>electron (100 eV)</text><text x='306' y='162' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>λ ≈ 0.12 nm</text><text x='14' y='184' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>ball (60 g, 50 m/s)</text><text x='306' y='184' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>λ ≈ 2×10⁻³⁴ m</text></svg>
cards.key: de Broglie proposed this in 1924, and experiment confirmed it in 1927. The greater the mass or speed, the shorter the wavelength.

cards.p: Light and electrons sometimes behave like waves and sometimes like particles. This is called wave-particle duality. By the uncertainty principle, position and momentum cannot both be known exactly at the same time: Δx·Δp ≥ h/4π.

cards.key: The Compton effect is also particle behavior. Uncertainty is not a flaw of the measuring device. It is a basic property of nature.

once.soru: In which event does light behave like a particle?

secenekler.neden: A single photon ejects a single electron. This is particle behavior.
Interference is wave behavior.
Diffraction is wave behavior.

cards.p: According to Bohr, the electron in hydrogen moves only in certain stable orbits and does not radiate while in them. The energy of the levels is En = −13.6/n² eV.

once.soru: In hydrogen, Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. What is E₂?

secenekler.neden: You divide by n², not by n.
Here it was multiplied instead of divided. It should be −13.6 / 4.

cards.h: Two ways to excite an atom
cards.p: A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly equals the difference between two levels. A colliding electron excites the atom if it arrives with energy equal to or greater than the difference, and moves on with the rest.

once.soru: In hydrogen the first excitation takes 10.2 eV and the second 12.1 eV. What happens if an 11 eV photon arrives?

secenekler.neden: A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly equals a level difference.
A photon cannot split its energy and leave the extra behind.
Ionization takes 13.6 eV.

cards.h: From Bohr to the modern atomic model
cards.p: The Bohr model could not explain atoms with many electrons. In the modern model the electron does not move in a definite orbit, and only the probability of finding it is known. A region where the probability is high is called an orbital.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='kuant-mod' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='80' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Bohr</text><text x='240' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Modern model</text><circle cx='80' cy='100' r='26' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1.2'/><circle cx='80' cy='100' r='46' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1.2'/><circle cx='80' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--c2)'/><circle cx='126' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--c1)'/><circle cx='240' cy='100' r='46' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.08'/><circle cx='240' cy='100' r='36' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.12'/><circle cx='240' cy='100' r='26' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.18'/><circle cx='240' cy='100' r='16' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.26'/><circle cx='240' cy='100' r='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35'/><circle cx='240' cy='100' r='4' fill='var(--c2)'/><path d='M140 100 H180' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none' marker-end='url(#kuant-mod)'/><text x='80' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>definite orbit</text><text x='80' y='182' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>(works for one-electron atoms)</text><text x='240' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>orbital: probability cloud</text><text x='240' y='182' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>(darker: higher probability)</text></svg>
cards.key: The energy levels are still quantized. You will see orbital types and filling order in the Chemistry topic Modern atomic theory.

once.soru: In the modern atomic model, what is known about where the electron is?

secenekler.neden: Because of the uncertainty principle, only where it may be found is known.
An exact orbit belonged to the Bohr model.
The regions where the probability is high (orbitals) are known.

cards.p: A solar cell produces current from photon energy, a photocell detects light, and an LED emits photons. A laser produces a narrow beam of one color with all waves in phase.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='14' y='14' width='140' height='80' rx='8' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c4)'/><text x='84' y='40' font-size='14' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Solar cell</text><text x='84' y='62' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>light → electricity</text><text x='84' y='80' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>photovoltaic effect</text><rect x='166' y='14' width='140' height='80' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='236' y='40' font-size='14' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Photocell</text><text x='236' y='62' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>detects light</text><text x='236' y='80' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>doors, streetlights</text><rect x='14' y='106' width='140' height='80' rx='8' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='84' y='132' font-size='14' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>LED</text><text x='84' y='154' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>electricity → light</text><text x='84' y='172' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>color: energy gap</text><rect x='166' y='106' width='140' height='80' rx='8' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='236' y='132' font-size='14' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Laser</text><text x='236' y='154' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>one color, in phase</text><text x='236' y='172' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>stimulated emission</text></svg>
cards.key: Photocells also control streetlights. A laser works by stimulated emission. The energy gap sets the color of an LED.

once.soru: An automatic door detects a person passing when a light beam is cut. Which device is used?

secenekler.neden: While light falls on the photocell, current flows. When the light is cut, the door opens.
A magnet does not detect light.
A thermometer measures temperature.

cards.p:
• Energy is quantized: E = h·f = h·c/λ.
• In the photoelectric effect, Ek,max = h·f − W = e·V0.
• Intensity changes only the current.
• For a photon p = h/λ, and for a matter wave λ = h/(m·v).
• In hydrogen, En = −13.6/n² eV.

quiz.q: Light of wavelength 310 nm falls on a metal whose work function is 2 eV. What voltage stops the ejected electrons (the stopping voltage), in volts? (h·c ≈ 1240 eV·nm)
quiz.e: The photon energy is 1240/310 = 4 eV. E<sub>k,max</sub> = 4 − 2 = 2 eV. Since e·V<sub>0</sub> = E<sub>k,max</sub>, V<sub>0</sub> = 2 V.

quiz.q: Only the intensity of light above the threshold frequency is increased. What happens to each quantity?
quiz.e: Intensity raises the number of photons arriving each second. More electrons are ejected and the current grows. Since the energy of each photon (h·f) stays the same, E<sub>k,max</sub> and the stopping voltage do not change. The threshold frequency depends on the metal.

quiz.q: Match each scientist with their contribution.
ciftler: Energy is exchanged in quantum packets
The scattered photon's wavelength gets longer
quiz.e: Planck showed that energy is exchanged in packets, and Compton that the wavelength of a scattered X-ray gets longer. de Broglie gave particles a wavelength, Heisenberg put forward the uncertainty principle, and Bohr the energy levels of hydrogen.

quiz.q: In the E<sub>k,max</sub>–f graph drawn for metals K and L, the two lines are parallel and L's line crosses the f axis at a higher frequency. Which is true?
o: L's line has a greater slope.
K has the higher threshold frequency.
For light of the same frequency, electrons from L have a greater E<sub>k,max</sub>.
L has the greater work function.
quiz.e: A metal with a higher threshold frequency also has a greater work function (W = h·f<sub>0</sub>). The slope is h for both metals. At the same f, L, with the greater W, has the smaller E<sub>k,max</sub>.
y: The slope of the lines equals Planck's constant. Since the lines are parallel, their slopes are the same.
The point where a line crosses the f axis is the threshold frequency. The higher threshold frequency belongs to L.
Electrons from L, which has the greater work function, come out with less energy. So E<sub>k,max</sub> is smaller.

radyoaktivite.title: The atomic nucleus and radioactivity
radyoaktivite.summary: Learn about the nucleus, binding energy, α, β and γ radiation, half-life, fission and fusion.

cards.p: The protons and neutrons in a nucleus are called nucleons. Z is the number of protons and A is the number of nucleons, so N = A − Z. Nuclei with the same Z but different A are called isotopes. 12C and 14C are an example.

cards.p: The force that holds the protons together is called the strong nuclear force. It acts between all nucleons, whatever their charge. Its range is very short. At about 1 fm it beats the repulsion, and a little farther out it drops to zero.

cards.key: 1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m. Neutrons add attraction without adding repulsion. That is why they matter for the stability of the nucleus.

cards.p: The mass of a nucleus is slightly less than the total mass of its nucleons. This difference is called the mass defect (Δm). When the nucleus forms, this mass is released as an energy of E = Δm·c². This energy is called the binding energy.

cards.p: The ratio of binding energy to nucleon number shows how tightly a nucleus is bound. The curve peaks around A ≈ 56-62 (about 8.8 MeV). For heavy nuclei it falls slowly.

cards.p: Alpha (α) radiation is a helium nucleus. In β⁻ decay a neutron turns into a proton, and in β⁺ decay a proton turns into a neutron. Gamma (γ) is a high-energy photon, and gamma emission does not change the element.

etk.soru: Match each decay with the change it makes in the nucleus.

once.soru: A nucleus emits alpha radiation. What comes out?

secenekler.neden: An alpha particle is 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
An electron comes out in β⁻ decay.
A high-energy photon is gamma radiation.

cards.p: In light, stable nuclei N/Z ≈ 1. Heavy nuclei need more neutrons to balance the repulsion of the protons, and the ratio approaches 1.5. All nuclei heavier than lead are radioactive.

once.soru: What does a nucleus with too many neutrons do to become stable?

secenekler.yazi: Turns a neutron into a proton
secenekler.neden: With β⁻ decay, N goes down and Z goes up. This fixes the ratio.
Absorbing a neutron makes the excess larger.
Gamma emission does not change N or Z. It only gets rid of energy.

cards.h: A and Z are conserved in the equation
cards.p: In a decay equation, the total A and the total Z are equal on both sides. α decay lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. β⁻ decay raises Z by 1. You find the number of α from the difference in A first, then the number of β from Z.

cards.h: Penetration and deflection in an electric field
cards.p: α radiation is stopped by paper, and β radiation by aluminum. γ is the most penetrating. In a magnetic field α and β⁻ bend in opposite directions, and the lighter β bends more. γ does not bend.

cards.p: The time it takes for half of the nuclei to decay is called the half-life (T½). With n = t / T½, the amount left is N = N₀ / 2n.

cards.p: When a living thing dies, it stops taking in new <sup>14</sup>C. The <sup>14</sup>C it has decreases with a half-life of about 5730 years. If the <sup>14</sup>C/<sup>12</sup>C ratio has dropped to a quarter, about 11 460 years have passed.

cards.key: While alive, the ratio is close to that of the atmosphere. The method is reliable only for samples that were once alive, up to ≈50 000 years.

once.soru: In a bone, the ¹⁴C ratio is half that of a living thing. The half-life is 5730 years. How old is the bone?

secenekler.neden: The ratio has halved once. That means one half-life.
That is two half-lives, and the ratio would have dropped to a quarter.
Dropping to half takes one full half-life.

cards.p: In fission a heavy nucleus such as 235U absorbs a neutron, splits and releases 2-3 neutrons. These neutrons start a chain reaction. In fusion, light nuclei join. Both release energy.

cards.p: Radiation is used in medicine for imaging and tumor treatment, in food preservation and in industry. Irradiated food does not become radioactive. To protect yourself, stay a short time, keep away and put shielding in between.

once.soru: Do strawberries preserved by irradiation become radioactive?

secenekler.neden: The radiation kills microbes but adds no radioactive material to the strawberries.
Being irradiated is not the same as being contaminated with radioactive material.
When the beam stops, its effect ends, and the strawberries do not radiate.

cards.p: The number of decays per second is called activity, and its unit is the becquerel (Bq). A person who is irradiated does not become radioactive. If radioactive material gets on or into the body, that is contamination.

once.soru: Does someone who had an X-ray taken give off radiation afterward?

secenekler.neden: A person who is irradiated does not become radioactive.
X-rays do not stay in the body.
There is no radiation unless radioactive material enters the body.

cards.p: Protons and neutrons are made of quarks. The u quark has charge +2/3 and the d quark −1/3. A proton is made of uud and a neutron of udd. The electron and the neutrino are leptons, which as far as we know cannot be split.

once.soru: A proton is made of uud quarks (u: +2/3, d: −1/3). What is its total charge?

secenekler.neden: 0 is the charge of the neutron (udd).
The d quark is negatively charged: 4/3 − 1/3 = 1.

cards.p: There are four fundamental forces: the strong, electromagnetic, weak and gravitational force. The weak force governs β decay. The forces are carried by gluons, photons, and W and Z bosons. The graviton has not been observed yet.

once.soru: Which force holds the nucleus together?

secenekler.neden: The strong force has a short range, but it is very strong. So it beats the repulsion of the protons.
At the scale of the nucleus, gravity is almost negligibly weak.
The electromagnetic force pushes the protons apart.

cards.p:
• Z is the number of protons, A−Z the number of neutrons.
• The strong force has a short range.
• E = Δm·c², and nuclei near iron are the most stable.
• α: A−4, Z−2. β⁻: Z+1, β⁺: Z−1.
• N = N₀/2ⁿ, and ¹⁴C gives the age.
• Fission and fusion release energy.

quiz.q: How many grams of 64 g of a radioactive substance with a half-life of 2 hours remain undecayed after 8 hours?
quiz.e: n = 8/2 = 4 half-lives pass. The amount left is 64/2<sup>4</sup> = 4 g.

quiz.q: Put each property with the radiation it belongs to.
quiz.e: Alpha is a helium nucleus. It is stopped by paper and lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. Beta minus is an electron. It raises Z by 1 and bends toward the positive plate. Gamma is an uncharged photon. It is not deflected and does not change A or Z.

quiz.q: According to the curve of binding energy per nucleon, does each reaction give energy or need energy?
quiz.e: The peak of the curve is around iron. Reactions that move toward the peak give energy. The fusion of light nuclei and the fission of heavy nuclei are examples. Splitting or fusing iron, which is at the peak, needs energy. Breaking a nucleus into its nucleons also needs energy.

quiz.q: A nucleus X emits first one alpha and then two beta minus particles in a row, turning into nucleus Y. Which is true for Y?
o: Its mass number is the same as X's
Its atomic number is 2 less than X's
It is an isobar of X
It is an isotope of X
quiz.e: Alpha emission lowers A by 4 and Z by 2. Two beta minus emissions raise Z by 2. In the end Z stays the same and A goes down by 4. Since the element is the same and the mass number is different, the new nucleus is an isotope.
y: Alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4. Beta emissions do not change it. So in total the mass number goes down by 4.
Alpha emission lowers the atomic number by 2, and two beta minus emissions raise it by 2. So the atomic number does not change.
An isobar is a nucleus with the same mass number. Since alpha emission lowers the mass number by 4, no isobar forms.
